pages.title: Character Creation
pages.summary: Create your character, determine their Core Scores, and learn about modifiers, Health, Defense Bonus, Character Points, Proficiency, and Reputation.
pages.body:
Character Creation

Every person out on the frontier has their strengths and weaknesses. In Dust & Blood, you'll determine yours by creating a character, establishing their abilities, and choosing how they develop over time. There ain't any traditional character classes to lock you into one way of life. You're free to make your character your own.

1. Core Scores

Now, the old doctors used to say a person's disposition depended on their humors. Blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm, they called 'em. Whether they were right about all that is another matter. But a person? Well, everyone has their own constitution, their own strengths, and their own weaknesses. Let's see what you've got to work with.

Every character in Dust & Blood has six Core Scores. These represent your character's abilities and help determine how well they perform different actions.

  • Might: Physical power and strength.
  • Agility: Speed, coordination, reflexes, and precision.
  • Condition: Physical toughness and endurance.
  • Intelligence: Reasoning, knowledge, education, and problem-solving.
  • Wisdom: Perception, judgment, instincts, and awareness.
  • Charisma: Personality, influence, confidence, and social ability.

Everybody has all six. What matters is how your scores measure up.

Rolling Core Scores

Let's see what you've been dealt. You'll roll for each of your six Core Scores before deciding where the results belong.

  1. Roll four six-sided dice (4d6).
  2. Discard the lowest die.
  3. Add the remaining three dice together.
  4. Repeat until you've rolled six results.

Once you've got all six results, assign them to Might, Agility, Condition, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma in whatever order you please. Put your best scores where they'll serve you well.

Core Score Modifiers

Your Core Scores tell you how capable your character is, but their modifiers are what you'll add to certain rolls. When making a d20 roll that uses a Core Score, add the appropriate modifier to your result.

Use the following formula to calculate your modifier:

Modifier = ⌊(Ability Score − 10) ÷ 2⌋

Round down to the nearest whole number. If you'd rather not do the arithmetic every time, use the table below.

Core ScoreModifier
1−5
2–3−4
4–5−3
6–7−2
8–9−1
10–11+0
12–13+1
14–15+2
16–17+3
18–19+4
20–21+5
22–23+6
24–25+7
26+8

Health

The frontier can be a hard place, and you'll want to know how much punishment your character can take. Your starting Health is determined by their Condition score.

Starting Health = 10 + Condition score

Whenever your character gains a level, they gain an additional 1d6 Health, unless a specific rule or ability changes how their Health is gained.

For more information about gaining levels and additional Health, see the Leveling Up section.

Defense Bonus (DB)

A good defense can keep you standing when trouble comes knocking. Your Defense Bonus (DB) represents your defense against attacks and is determined by the Defense Points (DP) provided by your equipped clothing.

Each piece of clothing contributes its own amount of DP. Add the DP of all equipped clothing together to determine your total DB.

Example: A character wearing ordinary traveler's clothing has a DB of 14, consisting of 7 DP from their shirt, 5 DP from their pants, and 2 DP from their hat.

Different clothing provides different amounts of DP, so what you wear matters. For details on clothing and equipment, see the Starting Equipment and Money section.

2. Character Points (CP)

Now that you've got your basic abilities sorted out, it's time to decide where your character's talents lie. Character Points (CP) are used to purchase improvements that help you develop your character.

CP can be spent on:

  • Ability Score Improvements (ASI): Increase your Core Scores.
  • Feats: Acquire additional character benefits.
  • Proficiencies: Gain training in skills, tools, weapons, and other areas.
  • Other Character Improvements: Purchase other available improvements according to their listed costs and requirements.

Every improvement has its own CP cost and requirements. Make sure you've got enough CP to pay for what you want, and that your character meets any requirements before making the purchase.

For the details on Feats, Traits, Flaws, and other improvements, consult their respective sections. Each has its own place in shaping the character you'll take out into the world.

Ability Score Improvements (ASI)

Sometimes a little extra strength, a sharper mind, or quicker reflexes can make all the difference. You can spend CP to improve your Core Scores.

For 3 CP, choose one of the following options:

  • Increase one Core Score by 2 points.
  • Increase two different Core Scores by 1 point each.

No Core Score can exceed 26.

You can purchase ASIs during character creation or later when permitted by the character advancement rules. For information about gaining additional CP as your character progresses, see the Leveling Up section.

3. Proficiencies and Proficiency Bonus

A little training goes a long way out here. Proficiency represents your character's training or specialized experience in a particular skill, tool, weapon, or saving throw.

When you make a roll that uses a proficiency you possess, add your Proficiency Bonus (PB) alongside the relevant Core Score modifier, as required by the rules for that roll.

For example, a character proficient in Animal Handling adds their PB to applicable checks involving handling or calming animals. A character without that proficiency adds only the relevant Core Score modifier, unless another rule grants an additional bonus.

Proficiency Bonus Rules

  • All characters begin with a Proficiency Bonus of +2.
  • Your PB represents your overall level of experience and increases as your character progresses.
  • Your PB is not determined by how many proficiencies you possess.
  • Add your PB only once to a roll, even if multiple proficiencies apply, unless a specific rule states otherwise.

You can acquire proficiencies through character options, CP purchases, and other rules that grant training. Each proficiency has its own requirements and acquisition rules, so check the relevant section before choosing one.

For information about acquiring additional proficiencies and how your PB changes with advancement, consult the relevant character improvement and Leveling Up sections.

4. Reputation

Out here, folks remember what you've done. Reputation represents how NPCs perceive, treat, and respond to your character. It reflects what people know or believe about you, and that ain't always the same as the truth.

Characters normally begin with 0 Reputation, although certain character options or game rules may modify this starting value.

Reputation ranges from −20 to +20, with 0 representing a character who has no notable reputation.

Negative Reputation

As your Reputation becomes more negative, NPCs may grow increasingly suspicious or hostile toward you. Shopkeepers might refuse service, strangers may be unwilling to help, and the authorities could take a greater interest in your business.

At −20 Reputation, your character is likely notorious nationwide. Reaching that point requires extraordinarily infamous actions, such as assassinating a president or committing other exceptionally serious acts that make your character a nationally recognized threat.

Ordinary crimes and everyday misbehavior aren't enough to earn that kind of infamy. A reputation that bad takes deeds that leave a lasting mark on the whole country.

Positive Reputation

A good name can open plenty of doors. As your Reputation becomes more positive, NPCs may become more willing to trust, respect, and assist you. You might receive better deals, gain access to new opportunities, or find people more willing to lend a hand.

At +20 Reputation, your character is exceptionally respected and trusted, potentially achieving nationwide fame through extraordinary deeds.

Changing Reputation

Reputation changes through your character's actions, accomplishments, and how others learn about them. What matters isn't just what you do, but what becomes known and who hears the story.

Remember, reputation ain't the same thing as morality. A character can be a decent soul with a terrible reputation, or a rotten one who's admired by half the country. The world judges you by what it believes about you, and out on the frontier, stories don't always tell the whole truth.

pages.summary: Choose Traits to improve your character or Flaws to gain additional Character Points at a cost.
pages.body:
Traits and Flaws

Now that you've got yourself an ordinary commoner, it's time to make your mark on the West.

Traits represent the skills, talents, and advantages that set your character apart. Some Traits have multiple ranks, with each rank providing a stronger benefit. The Character Point (CP) cost tells you how many points are required to purchase that rank.

Flaws represent weaknesses, bad habits, and troubles that follow your character around. Taking a Flaw grants Character Points, but it also comes with a mechanical drawback. Choose carefully; out on the frontier, even a small weakness can become a mighty problem.

pages.title: Backgrounds
pages.summary: Choose a Background to represent your character's past, training, and experience before setting out into the West.
pages.body:
Backgrounds

A Background tells the tale of the life your character led before setting out into the West. Whether they spent their days working a ranch, mending iron at a blacksmith's forge, or walking the lawless streets, their past has shaped the person they are today.

Each Background grants Proficiencies and Capabilities—the skills, knowledge, and experience your character picked up along the way. But every line of work has its hardships, and your past may come with a few disadvantages, too.

Background Description Proficiencies Capabilities Drawbacks or Requirements
Ranch Hand You've spent considerable time working with livestock, tending cattle, and handling horses. Animal Handling; Riding Hard Worker: +2 Might. Rough Hands: −3 Agility; Lost Opportunity: −2 Intelligence.
Blacksmith You've learned to work and shape metal at the forge, making and repairing the tools people depend on. Blacksmithing; Metalworking None specified. Rough Hands: −3 Agility; Socially Weird: −1 Charisma.
Lawyer You've worked with the law, whether arguing cases, interpreting statutes, or helping maintain order. Investigation; Intimidation Starting Reputation +5. Must have the Lawful alignment.
Gambler You've spent considerable time playing games of chance, reading people, and risking what you have for what you might win. Gambling; Deception None specified. Starting Debt: begin owing $20.
Outlaw You've survived beyond the protection of lawful society, relying on your wits and keeping out of sight. Stealth; Survival None specified. Wanted Man: starting Reputation −5.
Doctor You've received formal medical training and learned how to treat the sick and injured. Medicine; Herbalism None specified. Pacifist: disadvantage on firearm attacks.

Choosing a Background

Your Background represents the life you led before the campaign began. Choose the one that best reflects your character's history, training, and circumstances.

Backgrounds grant the Proficiencies and Capabilities listed above. Any listed drawback or requirement also applies to your character.

pages.summary: Track experience, gain Character Points, unlock higher Trait ranks, and improve your Proficiency Bonus as you advance.
pages.body:
Leveling Up

Out here in the West, nobody becomes a legend overnight. Every hard-fought gunfight, long journey, and lesson learned helps shape the person you'll become.

As your character earns Experience Points (XP), they gain levels. Each new level grants Character Points (CP) and may unlock new Trait ranks or increase your Proficiency Bonus.

pages.title: Starting Equipment and Money
pages.summary: Find the starting equipment kit and starting money your character receives from their Background.
pages.body:
Starting Equipment and Money

Before you ride out into the West, you'll need a few things to your name. Your Background determines the equipment you begin with and how much money you carry when the campaign begins.

You receive both the starting kit listed for your Background and its starting money. Your kit represents the tools, clothing, and supplies you've gathered from your life before the campaign begins.

Starting Equipment

Background Starting Kit
Ranch Hand Work clothes, bedroll, canteen, rope, work knife, saddle, bridle.
Blacksmith Work clothes, apron, blacksmith hammer, tongs, small tool kit, whetstone.
Lawman Lawman's badge, uniform or coat, handcuffs, notebook, writing supplies, watch.
Gambler Decent clothes, deck of cards, dice, small notebook, flask.
Outlaw Worn clothes, bedroll, canteen, rope, knife, lockpicks.
Doctor Doctor's bag, medical tools, bandages, antiseptic, surgical knife, notebook, watch.

Starting Money

Your Background also determines how much money you begin with. These amounts reflect the kind of work you've done and the circumstances you've lived under before setting out into the West.

Background Starting Money Why
Ranch Hand $10 Low-paid work, often compensated partly with food and lodging.
Blacksmith $25 A skilled trade with considerably higher wages.
Lawman $30 A stable paid position with better-than-laborer income.
Gambler $15 Unstable income; a gambler could have money one day and little the next.
Outlaw $5 Constantly moving makes it difficult to maintain savings.
Doctor $75 A highly skilled professional with substantially higher earning potential.

Getting Ready for the Trail

Your starting kit and money are separate benefits. You receive the listed equipment and the full amount of starting money for your Background.

You can use your money to purchase additional goods and supplies according to the prices listed in the equipment rules. Keep track of what you spend; out on the frontier, every dollar counts.

pages.title: The D20 System
pages.summary: Learn how d20 rolls, Difficulty Classes, advantage, disadvantage, modifiers, and Skill Checks work in Dust & Blood.
pages.body:
The D20: How the West Works

Dust & Blood runs on a twenty-sided die, commonly called a d20. Before we get into the finer points of the game, let's go over what that means and how you'll use it at the table.

Rolling the Dice

A d20 has twenty sides, numbered 1 through 20. Each number has an equal 5% chance of coming up. Whenever your character attempts something with an uncertain outcome—like sneaking past a guard, picking a lock, or shooting a gunslinger—you may be called on to roll a d20.

Your Game Master (GM) sets a Difficulty Class (DC) based on how hard the task is. Roll the die, add any applicable modifiers, and compare your total to the DC. If your total meets or exceeds the DC, you succeed. If it falls short, you fail.

Of course, the trail ain't always that straightforward. Sometimes you'll have the advantage, and sometimes the odds will be stacked against you.

Advantage and Disadvantage

Certain situations, Traits, or Flaws can give you Advantage or Disadvantage on a roll. Unless a rule specifically says otherwise, your GM will determine when these apply.

Rule How It Works
Advantage Roll two d20s and keep the higher result.
Disadvantage Roll two d20s and keep the lower result.

Advantage gives you a better shot at success, while Disadvantage makes things harder. Neither changes the die itself; they simply change which result you use.

Modifiers: Putting Your Experience to Work

A die roll is only part of the story. Your character's abilities and experience matter, too.

Every Core Score grants a Modifier. When you attempt an action that calls for one of these modifiers, add the appropriate number to your d20 roll. Depending on the situation, Traits, Flaws, and other rules may grant additional bonuses or penalties.

In other words, a seasoned gunslinger has a few more tricks up their sleeve than some greenhorn fresh off the train.

Example: A Sure-Shot

Take the Trait Uncle Sam Will Be Proud, which grants a +3 bonus to firearm Hit Rolls at Rank I.

Say you're taking a shot at an enemy. You roll a d20 and get a 17. Add your +3 bonus from the Trait, along with any other applicable modifiers, and your total becomes 20 or higher if those additional modifiers contribute at least 0.

That bonus represents your character's training and ability with firearms. A good roll helps, but knowing how to handle a gun can make all the difference when the lead starts flying.

Skill Checks: Can You Get the Job Done?

Not every challenge in the West can be settled with a bullet. Sometimes you need a steady hand, a sharp mind, or a little good sense.

Skill Checks determine whether your character can pull off an uncertain task. Whether you're tracking a fugitive across open country, treating a wounded companion, or trying to talk your way past a suspicious lawman, a Skill Check puts your character's abilities to the test.

When a Skill Check is called for, roll a d20 and add the applicable modifiers. Your GM determines the DC, and your total decides whether you get the job done.

Remember: a roll doesn't guarantee success, and a failed roll doesn't mean the story stops. It just means the West has thrown another problem your way.

The Basic Roll

When a rule calls for a d20 check, use this general formula:

Total = d20 roll + applicable modifiers

Compare the total to the DC set by the GM. Meeting or beating the DC means success; rolling below it means failure, unless a specific rule says otherwise.

pages.title: Combat System
pages.summary: Learn how combat works in Dust & Blood, including Action Points, firearms, hit locations, melee attacks, grappling, cover, and weapon handling.
pages.body:
Core Combat System

Core Resolution

The West is full of uncertain outcomes. A shot might find its mark, a desperate escape might fail, and even the most experienced gunslinger can have a bad day.

Dust & Blood uses a d20 as its primary resolution die. Whenever a character attempts an action with a meaningful chance of success or failure, they roll a d20 and apply the appropriate modifiers.

The Game Master (GM) determines the applicable Difficulty Class (DC) or defensive value, and the player resolves the action using the relevant rules. From shootouts in dusty streets to desperate struggles in the wilderness, this system governs combat, ability checks, and other uncertain actions throughout the game.

Action Points (AP)

Every second counts when lead starts flying. Action Points (AP) determine how much a character can accomplish during combat and other situations where timing matters.

AP can be spent on movement, firing weapons, drawing or holstering weapons, reloading, taking cover, interacting with objects, climbing, and other actions. Spend them wisely; the opportunity you pass up today might be the one you need tomorrow.

Characters regenerate AP at the start of their active turns. Unused AP can be saved for future turns, allowing a character to prepare for the next opportunity instead of spending everything at once.

A character can hold a maximum of 12 AP at any given time.

Turn Definitions

  • Active Turn: The turn currently belonging to your character.
  • Inactive Turn: Any turn belonging to another character.

AP Regeneration

At the start of each active turn, a character regenerates 3 AP. These AP are added to any AP the character has saved from previous turns, up to the maximum of 12 AP.

For example, a character with 3 AP saved gains another 3 AP at the start of their next active turn, giving them 6 AP.

Characters regenerate AP even while unconscious. However, an unconscious character cannot spend those AP to perform actions.

Live Combat

A gunfight doesn't always wait for your turn. Live Combat allows characters to spend their available AP outside their active turns. During another character's turn, a player may spend AP on permitted actions to react to changes on the battlefield.

During an inactive turn, characters may move on foot or by mount, take cover, and interact with the world. Firearm attacks can only be made during a character's own active turn.

Any AP spent during an inactive turn is deducted from the character's available AP.

Actions

Not everything a cowboy does costs AP. Talking and activating Parley do not require AP, although an enemy is under no obligation to negotiate.

Actions that require AP include:

  • Movement.
  • Firing a weapon.
  • Reloading.
  • Drawing or holstering a weapon.
  • Taking cover.
  • Sneaking.
  • Mounting or dismounting a horse.
  • Lassoing.
  • Interacting with objects.
  • Climbing.
  • Other actions designated by the GM.

AP costs apply primarily during combat, but the GM may also use them in tense situations outside combat, such as chases, timed challenges, or puzzles.

The GM determines whether an action requires AP when the situation demands precise timing. When every second counts, knowing what you can accomplish before the clock runs out can make all the difference.

Firearms

Hit Rolls

In a gunfight, landing a shot and deciding where it lands are two different matters. Firearm attacks use two separate d20 rolls: the Hit Roll and the Location Roll.

The Hit Roll determines whether an attack successfully strikes its target. If the Hit Roll succeeds, the attacker makes a Location Roll to determine which body part is struck.

If the Hit Roll fails, no Location Roll is made.

Hit Roll Modifier

A steady hand and quick reflexes can make a difference when a bullet is on the line. A character's Hit Roll Modifier is calculated by subtracting 2 from their Agility modifier.

Hit Roll Modifier = Agility Modifier − 2

For example:

  • An Agility modifier of +5 gives a Hit Roll Modifier of +3.
  • An Agility modifier of +2 gives a Hit Roll Modifier of 0.
  • An Agility modifier of 0 gives a Hit Roll Modifier of −2.

Apply the resulting modifier to the Hit Roll, along with any applicable weapon bonuses, proficiency bonuses, traits, gun modifications, and other effects.

A character's Agility matters, but it is only part of the equation. Training, equipment, and the right modifications can turn an ordinary firearm into a formidable tool.

Firing

Pulling the trigger costs 1 AP, regardless of whether the attack hits or misses.

Reloading

A firearm is only useful while it has ammunition. Reloading costs vary depending on the firearm. Consult Weapons and Items for the specific AP cost required to reload each weapon.

Defense Bonus (DB)

A target's Defense Bonus (DB) represents the number an attacker must meet or exceed with their final Hit Roll to successfully hit them.

Roll a d20 and apply the appropriate modifiers. If the final result equals or exceeds the target's DB, the attack hits, and the attacker makes a Location Roll.

If the final result is lower than the target's DB, the attack misses.

In a firefight, every shot counts. Your target's DB tells you just how difficult they are to hit, so make sure you account for the bonuses and penalties that apply before deciding whether to take the shot.

Hit Location

A successful shot doesn't tell the whole story. Once a firearm Hit Roll succeeds, roll a d20 to determine where the attack strikes.

Location RollBody PartEffect
1HeadThe target is killed instantly unless they have head protection. If protected, they take the firearm's normal damage instead.
2–5ArmsThe target drops whatever they are holding and makes a DC 9 Condition Check. On a failure, the struck arm is incapacitated and cannot be used. On a success, the arm remains functional.
6–9LegsThe target makes a DC 9 Condition Check. On a failure, the struck leg is incapacitated and the target's movement speed is halved. On a success, the leg remains functional and movement is unaffected.
10–20TorsoRoll the weapon's damage normally.

Each location serves a different purpose in combat: the head is lethal, the torso deals damage, the arms impair utility, and the legs impair mobility.

Head protection prevents the instant-kill effect described above and causes the target to take the firearm's normal damage instead.

Mounted Combat

A horse can carry you across open country, but firing accurately from the saddle is another matter.

When firing a firearm while riding a horse, the attack is made with disadvantage.

A character riding a horse cannot declare a Targeted Shot. Mounted firearm attacks therefore rely on the normal Hit Roll and Location Roll system.

Weapon-specific bonuses and penalties still apply unless another rule states otherwise.

Condition Checks

Not every wound puts a cowboy out of the fight. Sometimes the question is whether they can push through the pain and keep going.

A Condition Check is an ability check using the character's Condition modifier.

The standard Condition Check difficulty is DC 5. Firearm injuries to the arms and legs specifically use DC 9.

The character rolls a d20, applies the appropriate modifier, and compares the result against the DC. A result meeting or exceeding the DC succeeds.

For firearm injuries to the arms and legs, the Condition Check determines whether the injury causes its associated impairment. A successful check means the associated impairment does not occur.

Knives

Not every confrontation calls for a firearm. Knives are close-range weapons that offer an alternative for characters who prefer fighting up close or taking a quieter approach when circumstances allow.

Knives are not intended to compete with firearms in raw damage. Instead, they offer a versatile option for close combat, with different attacks serving different purposes.

Knives also provide access to Release, which allows a character to attempt to cut themselves free from a lasso.

Knife attacks use the same Hit Roll system as firearms. If the Hit Roll succeeds, the attacker rolls for hit location. The effects depend on the location struck and the type of knife attack performed.

Knife Hit Locations

When a knife attack hits, roll a d20 to determine the location struck.

Location RollBody PartEffect
1–7Arms (35%)The target drops whatever they are holding and makes a DC 9 Condition Check. On a failure, the struck arm is incapacitated and cannot be used. On a success, the arm remains functional.
8–14Legs (35%)The target makes a DC 5 Condition Check. On a failure, the struck leg is incapacitated and the target's movement speed is halved. On a success, the leg remains functional and movement is unaffected.
15–20Torso (30%)Apply damage according to the type of knife attack performed.

Slashing

A slashing attack that strikes the torso deals 1d4 damage and inflicts the Bleeding condition.

While bleeding, the target takes an additional 1d4 damage at the start of each of their active turns until the wound is bandaged.

Bleeding applies only to torso hits.

Stabbing

A stabbing attack that strikes the torso deals 1d6 damage and causes little to no recurring bleeding.

If the Location Roll indicates the arms or legs, the attack does not connect with the torso, and the normal stabbing damage is not applied. The target instead makes a DC 14 Condition Check to determine whether the associated limb impairment occurs.

Slit Throat

When sneaking behind a target, a character may declare that they are attempting to slit the target's throat.

The attempt succeeds only on a natural 20 on the Hit Roll and serves as the knife equivalent of a firearm headshot.

The action can be heard by anyone within a 10-foot radius. Because this is a declared action, the attacker must announce their intention before rolling.

Release

Getting caught by a lasso doesn't necessarily mean you're staying caught. A character equipped with a knife can attempt to cut themselves free from a lasso without spending AP.

The character must succeed on a DC 5 Condition Check to escape. This action costs no AP.

Grappling

Sometimes a fight gets too close for a clean shot. Grappling allows characters to tackle, restrain, or otherwise control an opponent instead of relying on weapons alone.

There are two types of grappling: Physical Grappling and Lasso Grappling.

Physical Grappling

A Physical Grapple represents directly controlling another character, such as tackling them or restraining their arms.

To initiate a Physical Grapple, the attacker makes a Might Check against a DC equal to the target's Might score. If the attacker succeeds, the target becomes Physically Grappled.

Escaping depends on the strength of the two combatants.

If the grappled character has higher Might than the grappler, they automatically overcome the grapple. If their Might is equal to or lower than the grappler's, they must succeed on a DC 10 Might Check to escape.

Lasso Grappling

A lasso gives a character another way to control an opponent, especially at a distance.

A Lasso Grapple costs 2 AP and requires a Hit Roll against the target's DB.

If the Hit Roll succeeds, both characters roll a d20 and add their Agility modifiers. If the attacker's total is higher, the target becomes Lassoed.

A Lassoed character cannot move freely.

A character equipped with a knife may use Release to attempt to cut the lasso. Without an equipped knife, the character must spend 3 AP and succeed on a DC 15 Might Check to escape.

The attacker may spend 1 AP to pull the target 5 feet closer. The attacker does not need to physically hold the lasso to maintain the grapple.

Punching and Physical Attacks

Not every fight starts with a gun being drawn. Sometimes the trouble begins with a fist.

Punching and other unarmed physical attacks require the attacker to be within 5 feet of their opponent.

To determine whether an unarmed attack hits, roll against the target's Defense Class (DC) divided by 2.

Unarmed damage is calculated by dividing the attacker's Might score by the result of a 1d6 roll.

Making one punch costs 1 AP. Each punch requires its own attack roll and damage roll.

Cover

In the West, a good piece of cover can be the difference between walking away and becoming part of the scenery. In Dust & Blood, cover protects specific parts of a character's body rather than making them harder to hit overall.

When attacking an enemy behind cover, roll the Hit Roll normally. If the attack hits, roll for Hit Location as usual.

If the body part rolled is protected by cover, the shot hits the cover instead, and the target takes no damage from that attack.

If the body part is exposed, the attack hits the target normally.

The GM determines which body parts are protected by a particular piece of cover based on the character's position and the surrounding environment. A low wall might protect the legs, while a larger barrier could shield more of the body.

Always pay attention to what's between you and your target. A good shot means little if all you hit is a fencepost.

Gun Handling

A firearm isn't always something you can simply pick up and fire. Every firearm has a minimum required number of hands to use. Certain Traits may alter these requirements; consult the relevant Trait rules.

For example, if a weapon requires two hands, a character cannot use that weapon while performing an activity that occupies one or both hands, such as climbing a ladder or leading a horse, unless a rule or Trait permits it.

Before heading into a fight, make sure your weapon suits the situation. The right firearm won't do you much good if your hands are already occupied.

Braced Rifles

A steady rifle is a more accurate rifle. When a character goes prone and braces a rifle against the ground, or mounts it on a stable surface such as a windowsill, they gain a +5 bonus to Hit Rolls.

This bonus applies only to rifles.

Helping Hand

The West can be a hard place to make it alone. When a character assists an ally with an Ability Check, the assisting character rolls 4d6.

Convert the total rolled into its corresponding modifier using the same rules used during character creation. Apply that modifier to the ally's Ability Check, adding it if positive or subtracting it if negative.

A high roll can improve the ally's chances of success, while a low roll can hinder them. Lending a hand can make the difference, but it doesn't guarantee the job gets done.

Weapon Proficiency

Experience is earned one way or another, but practice makes a difference when the stakes are high.

A character gains proficiency with a weapon by training with it during downtime or earning more than 100 XP with that weapon.

When making a Hit Roll with a weapon the character is proficient with, add the character's Proficiency Bonus to the roll.

Gun Modifications

A firearm can be more than the sum of its parts. With the right modifications, a character can tailor a weapon to their preferred way of fighting.

Every firearm has three modification slots that can be filled with different gun modifications to improve its performance.

Modifications grant specific mechanical bonuses, such as reducing AP costs, improving accuracy, increasing ammunition capacity, or improving reload speed.

Modifications can be interchanged during downtime, allowing players to customize their firearms to suit their preferred playstyle.

Each modification provides a distinct benefit, giving players the freedom to build their weapons around different combat approaches. Whether you favor speed, precision, or capacity, the right setup can give you an edge when the shooting starts.

Weapon Type Tables

Not every firearm handles the same way. Weapon types determine a firearm's handling characteristics, required hands, and special benefits or drawbacks.

Apply the listed bonuses and penalties whenever their stated conditions are met. When choosing a weapon, consider not just how hard it hits, but how it handles, how quickly you can reload it, and the distances at which it performs best.

pages.title: Fishing
pages.summary: Learn how to fish in Dust & Blood, identify freshwater catches, determine fish sizes, and calculate their selling prices.
pages.body:
Fishing in the West

There's more than cattle and game to be found out on the frontier. A quiet lake or a bend in the river can provide a welcome meal—or a little extra money for the trail. In Dust & Blood, fishing is resolved with three dice rolls: one to determine whether you catch anything, one to identify the fish, and one to determine its size and value.

Required Equipment: You must have a fishing pole and bait or a lure to fish.

How Fishing Works

First, roll a d20 against the lake's Fishing DC. Your result must be higher than the DC to catch a fish. A result equal to or below the DC means the attempt fails.

If you succeed, roll a d20 on the Freshwater Fish Table to determine the species you catch. Then roll a d12 on the Fish Size Table to determine its size category and selling price modifier.

Multiply the fish's base selling price by its size modifier to determine its final selling price. The GM determines the fish's actual length and weight based on its species and size category.

Fishing Rules

You must have a fishing pole with bait or a lure to fish.

  1. Roll a d20 against the lake's Fishing DC. You must roll higher than the DC to catch a fish.
  2. If successful, roll a d20 on the Freshwater Fish Table.
  3. Roll a d12 on the Fish Size Table to determine the fish's size category.
  4. Multiply the fish's base selling price by its size modifier to determine its final value.
  5. The GM determines each fish's actual length and weight based on its species and size category.

Example Catch

You fish in a lake with a Fishing DC of 10 and roll a 15. Since 15 is higher than 10, you successfully catch a fish.

You then roll a 9 on the Freshwater Fish Table, catching a Brown Trout with a base selling price of $0.45. Your d12 size roll is 10, making it Very Large. Its base price is multiplied by 2:

$0.45 × 2 = $0.90

Your Very Large Brown Trout is worth $0.90. Not a fortune, but every dollar counts when you're making your way out West.

Foraging in the West

The frontier offers more than cattle, game, and open land. For those who know where to look, the wilderness holds herbs and plants that can be gathered for use along the trail. A sharp eye and a little luck can turn an ordinary walk through the woods into a useful find.

How Foraging Works

Foraging in Dust & Blood is resolved through three dice rolls. First, the player rolls a d20 to beat the Foraging DC assigned to the forest. If the roll exceeds the DC, the attempt succeeds. Otherwise, the character finds nothing.

On a successful foraging check, the player rolls a d20 on the Plant Species Table to determine which plant they discover. Once the plant species has been determined, the player rolls a d4 on the Purity Table to establish the purity of the gathered plant.

Plant Species Table

After succeeding on a foraging check, roll a d20 and consult the following table to determine which plant the character finds.

Foraging Rules

  1. The GM assigns a Foraging DC based on the forest and surrounding conditions.
  2. The player rolls a d20. The roll must exceed the DC for the attempt to succeed.
  3. On a success, the player rolls a d20 on the Plant Species Table.
  4. The player then rolls a d4 on the Plant Purity Table.
  5. The character gathers the plant species and purity determined by the rolls.

The wilderness can be generous, but it does not give up its secrets to everyone. Watch your step, keep your eyes open, and make every trip into the woods count.

pages.title: GM Resources
pages.summary: A practical guide to building settings, setting DCs, running NPCs, balancing encounters, creating adventures, and leading a Dust & Blood campaign.
pages.body:
GM Resources

Every town has a story. Every outlaw has a reason. And every trail leads somewhere.

Being the Game Master (GM) means bringing the world of Dust & Blood to life. You control the towns, the people, the dangers, and the consequences of the players' choices. You describe what the characters see, decide how the world responds to their actions, and help shape the story as it unfolds.

You don't need to plan every little detail. A good GM prepares enough to make the world feel real, then lets the players leave their mark on it.

This section contains the tools, guidelines, and advice needed to run a game of Dust & Blood, whether you're managing a quiet frontier town or a territory filled with outlaws, dangerous wildlife, and unfinished business.

1. Building Your Setting

Before the first gun is drawn, give your players somewhere worth visiting.

A setting doesn't need a massive map, dozens of towns, or a detailed history stretching back centuries. Start small. A single town, a handful of interesting characters, and a problem that needs solving are enough to begin a campaign.

Step 1: Choose Your Territory

Decide where your campaign takes place. Consider the landscape, weather, wildlife, settlements, and dangers of the region.

  • Open Prairie: Wide grasslands, scattered ranches, grazing cattle, and long stretches of lonely trail.
  • Mountain Country: Steep passes, isolated settlements, mining camps, and dangerous travel.
  • Desert Country: Water shortages, harsh weather, remote homesteads, and scarce supplies.
  • Woodland Frontier: Dense forests, hunting grounds, rivers, and settlements separated by wilderness.
  • River Country: Trading posts, ferries, busy docks, and towns built around the water.

Mix these environments as needed. The West is a big place, and not every stretch of country looks the same.

Step 2: Build a Starting Town

Your players need a place to buy supplies, meet people, hear rumors, and find trouble.

A starting town should have at least:

  • A General Store: Food, supplies, tools, and everyday equipment.
  • A Gunsmith: Firearms, ammunition, repairs, and weapon-related services.
  • A Blacksmith: Horseshoes, metalwork, repairs, and forged goods.
  • A Doctor: Medical treatment and a place to recover from serious injuries.
  • A Saloon: Drinks, conversation, rumors, and the occasional dispute.
  • A Law Office: A sheriff, deputy, marshal, or other local authority.
  • A Stable: Horses, boarding, feed, and riding equipment.

You don't need to prepare every shop's inventory. Decide what is available when the players visit, using the game's equipment prices and rules.

Step 3: Give the Town a Problem

A town becomes interesting when something threatens its ordinary life.

  • An outlaw gang has been robbing travelers on the main road.
  • Two ranching families are fighting over a disputed property line.
  • A local mine has stopped paying its workers.
  • A cattle herd has disappeared during the night.
  • A bounty hunter has arrived looking for someone the townsfolk are protecting.
  • A series of strange disappearances has left the settlement afraid to travel after dark.

A good starting problem gives the players something to investigate, someone to talk to, and a reason to take action.

Step 4: Decide Who Holds the Power

Every settlement has people who influence what happens there.

Ask yourself:

  • Who enforces the law?
  • Who owns the most land or controls the most money?
  • Who do ordinary townsfolk trust?
  • Who is feared?
  • Who benefits from the town's current troubles?

These people don't need to be villains. A sheriff might be honest but outnumbered, while a wealthy rancher might genuinely believe their actions are necessary.

Conflicting interests make a setting feel alive.

2. Setting Difficulty Classes (DCs)

A Difficulty Class (DC) represents how difficult an action is to accomplish. When a character attempts something uncertain, the GM determines the appropriate DC using the Core Rules.

Choose a DC based on the task itself, the circumstances, and the consequences of failure. Do not raise a DC simply because you want the players to fail.

Suggested DC Guidelines

Use the following table as a starting point when setting DCs. These are suggested guidelines for GMs, not replacements for any specific DCs already established by the rules.

DifficultySuggested DCExample
Very Easy5Climb a sturdy ladder or find an obvious object.
Easy10Calm a nervous horse or climb a rough fence.
Moderate12Track someone across disturbed ground or pick a simple lock.
Challenging15Convince a suspicious stranger or climb a difficult rock face.
Hard18Follow faint tracks through poor conditions or pick a complex lock.
Very Hard20Persuade a hostile witness to cooperate or cross a dangerous route.
Nearly Impossible25Accomplish an extraordinary feat under severe pressure.
Legendary30Attempt something beyond ordinary human capability.

Use the game's applicable roll formula and modifiers when resolving the check. The DC is the target the character must meet or exceed if the relevant rule uses that convention.

What Affects a DC?

Consider these factors before choosing a number:

  • Conditions: Is it dark, raining, windy, or unusually noisy?
  • Equipment: Does the character have the proper tools, supplies, or equipment?
  • Time: Can the character take their time, or must they act immediately?
  • Opposition: Is someone actively resisting the attempt?
  • Preparation: Has the character gathered information or made arrangements that improve their chances?
  • Consequences: Would failure create a minor inconvenience, or could it put the character in serious danger?

Apply bonuses, penalties, advantage, disadvantage, or other adjustments only when supported by the game's rules. Don't invent extra modifiers when the normal check already accounts for the situation.

When Not to Roll

Not every action needs a check.

If a character performs an ordinary task with the proper tools and no meaningful obstacle, simply let them succeed.

For example, opening an unlocked door doesn't require a roll. Opening a locked door while an outlaw approaches might.

Call for a roll when the outcome is uncertain and the result matters to the story.

Failure Should Move the Story Forward

Failure doesn't always have to mean nothing happens.

A failed check might:

  • Cost valuable time.
  • Alert a nearby guard.
  • Damage a useful tool.
  • Give an NPC a reason to distrust the characters.
  • Force the party to find another route.
  • Create a new problem that must be addressed.

Use consequences that fit the situation. A failed attempt to negotiate shouldn't automatically lead to a gunfight, and a failed tracking check doesn't have to end the adventure.

3. Running NPCs

Non-player characters (NPCs) are the people who inhabit your world. They can be helpful, hostile, frightened, greedy, stubborn, or anything else that suits the story.

You don't need a full character sheet for every person the players meet.

For an ordinary NPC, decide three things:

1. What do they want? Money, safety, justice, revenge, or something else?

2. What do they know? Information about the town, the local trouble, or the people involved.

3. How do they treat strangers? Are they friendly, suspicious, indifferent, or openly hostile?

For important NPCs, add a name, a memorable trait, a personal goal, and a secret or complication.

Making NPCs Feel Real

Give each NPC a reason for behaving the way they do. A shopkeeper might refuse to extend credit because the last person who borrowed money never returned. A sheriff might hesitate to arrest a powerful rancher because the town depends on the ranch's workers.

NPCs should respond to what the characters actually do. Helping someone may earn their trust, while threatening or cheating them may create lasting consequences.

Use the appropriate adversary statistics when an NPC enters a situation that requires them. Do not give every townsfolk member the combat abilities of a trained gunfighter.

4. Creating Encounters

An encounter is any situation that requires the players to make meaningful decisions. Encounters can involve combat, investigation, negotiation, travel, or survival.

A good campaign uses a mixture of encounter types.

  • Combat Encounters: Outlaws ambush the party, a bounty hunter confronts a fugitive, or a dangerous animal protects its territory.
  • Social Encounters: A sheriff questions the characters, a rancher offers a job, or a witness refuses to speak.
  • Investigation Encounters: The players search a crime scene, follow tracks, examine a suspicious shipment, or uncover a local secret.
  • Travel Encounters: A washed-out bridge, a broken wagon, severe weather, or an unexpected delay forces the party to make a decision.
  • Survival Encounters: The characters must find water, protect their supplies, navigate unfamiliar territory, or deal with a threat in the wilderness.

Balancing Combat

When building a fight, consider more than the number of enemies.

  • The enemies' health, Defense, weapons, and damage.
  • The number of player characters.
  • Available cover and escape routes.
  • Starting distance and visibility.
  • Whether the enemies have a tactical advantage.
  • Whether the players have already spent resources.
  • Whether surrender, negotiation, or retreat is possible.

Use the adversary statistics in the game as your baseline. A group of enemies with strong weapons and good cover may be more dangerous than a larger group caught in the open.

Don't assume every encounter must be a fair fight. The players should have enough information to make meaningful decisions, and they should be able to retreat from situations that are beyond them when the circumstances permit.

5. Designing Quests and Adventures

An adventure begins with a problem, develops through player decisions, and ends when those decisions produce a meaningful outcome.

A simple adventure can be prepared using five parts:

1. The Hook: Give the characters a reason to get involved.

2. The Problem: Establish what is happening and why it matters.

3. The Leads: Provide people, clues, locations, or evidence the players can investigate.

4. The Complication: Introduce new information or a difficult choice.

5. The Resolution: Let the players determine how the situation ends.

Example: Trouble on the Cattle Trail

The Hook: A rancher offers the party $50 to find a missing herd.

The Problem: The cattle vanished during the night, and the rancher suspects a rival.

The Leads: The characters can question ranch hands, inspect the pasture, or follow tracks toward an abandoned trail.

The Complication: The trail suggests that the cattle were moved by someone familiar with the ranch. The supposed rival may not be responsible.

The Resolution: The players decide whether to expose the culprit, negotiate a return of the herd, pursue the cattle, or accept a different arrangement.

The details can change depending on what the players discover. Prepare possibilities, not a single mandatory sequence of events.

6. Managing Money, Rewards, and Supplies

Money gives the players a reason to work, save, negotiate, and make difficult choices.

When offering a reward, consider the danger involved, the time required, the cost of supplies, and the party's current resources.

Rewards might include:

  • Cash or a bounty payment.
  • Weapons, ammunition, or equipment.
  • A horse or access to a stable.
  • Information, introductions, or useful contacts.
  • A place to stay or supplies for the journey.
  • Reputation, favors, or future opportunities.

Use the established prices in the equipment and services lists. If a reward would make the party unusually wealthy compared with the game's economy, consider whether that is intentional.

Not every reward needs to be money. A trusted sheriff may provide information that would otherwise take days to uncover.

7. Handling Unexpected Player Choices

Players will regularly do things you didn't plan for. This is normal, and it is part of what makes a tabletop roleplaying game enjoyable.

When the party tries something unexpected:

  1. Listen to the plan. Let the players explain what they want to accomplish.
  2. Determine what stands in their way. Identify the obstacle, opposition, or risk.
  3. Check the rules. Use the existing rule that best fits the situation.
  4. Set a fair difficulty. Consider the circumstances and the characters' preparation.
  5. Resolve the outcome. Describe what happens and how the world responds.

If you don't know a rule, make a reasonable temporary ruling, explain it clearly, and keep the game moving. Check the written rule after the session if necessary, then use a consistent approach going forward.

Never punish players simply because their ideas differ from your plans. The GM's job is to present the world and its consequences, not to force the players down one path.

8. Keeping the Game Moving

A good session needs room for conversation, planning, exploration, and action. Too much preparation can slow the game just as much as too little.

  • Describe what matters. Focus on details the characters can see, hear, use, or investigate.
  • Give players choices. Offer meaningful options without deciding for them.
  • Keep information consistent. Important clues should not change simply because the players guessed incorrectly.
  • Let preparation pay off. Reward clever plans and useful equipment when they genuinely help.
  • Make consequences understandable. Players should generally be able to recognize obvious dangers before committing to a risky choice.
  • Share the spotlight. Give every player opportunities to contribute.
  • Take short breaks when needed. A brief pause can help everyone regroup and enjoy the session.

When Players Get Stuck

If the party cannot figure out what to do next, don't immediately reveal the entire solution.

Instead, consider:

  • Having an NPC mention a useful lead.
  • Letting the characters notice a clue they previously overlooked.
  • Introducing a new event that changes the situation.
  • Reminding players of information their characters already know.

The goal is to help the adventure continue without removing the players' ability to solve the problem themselves.

9. Preparing Your First Session

You do not need an entire world prepared before you begin. For your first session, prepare the essentials.

Use this checklist:

  • Choose a region and describe its general atmosphere.
  • Create one starting town or settlement.
  • Prepare three to five memorable NPCs.
  • Establish one main problem or adventure hook.
  • Decide where the party can investigate or travel.
  • Prepare appropriate adversary statistics if combat is likely.
  • Check relevant equipment prices and available services.
  • Think of two or three possible complications.
  • Decide what the players can gain if they succeed.
  • Leave room for the players to surprise you.

Once the players begin making decisions, build on what happens at the table. Their actions may create new allies, enemies, locations, and stories worth exploring.

10. The Golden Rule of the West

Be fair, be consistent, and let the players shape the story.

The GM doesn't need to defeat the players, protect them from every consequence, or predict every decision. Your responsibility is to present an interesting world, apply the rules consistently, and give the players meaningful opportunities to change their circumstances.

Sometimes the party will save a town. Sometimes they'll make a terrible deal, lose a valuable lead, or discover that the law is not always on their side.

Let those outcomes matter.

The frontier is a place of opportunity, danger, and hard choices. Make the world believable, give the players room to act, and let the story unfold from there.

After all, out here, nobody gets to decide how the trail ends until the journey is done.

pages.title: Mounts
pages.summary: Learn how to create, train, ride, equip, and care for horses and oxen in Dust & Blood.
pages.body:
Mounts of the West

Mounts are a big part of Dust & Blood. Horses carry riders across the open frontier, help ranchers move cattle, and provide speed when trouble is close behind. Oxen serve a different purpose, hauling wagons, pulling heavy supplies, and working the land. Both require their own statistics, equipment, training, and care.

Live mounts such as horses and oxen require their own character sheets. The following rules explain how to create them, determine their abilities, and manage them throughout an adventure.

Horses

1. Horse Creation

Create a horse using these steps:

  1. Choose a breed and apply its attribute bonuses.
  2. Roll 1d6 for individual quality.
  3. Choose or roll its temperament.
  4. Calculate HP, DB, speed, stamina, and carrying capacity.
  5. Choose its training.
  6. Record its identification, equipment, and price.

Horses use the same six attributes and modifiers as characters: Might, Agility, Condition, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

Individual Quality

Roll 1d6 after applying breed bonuses.

RollEffect
1Primary attribute -1
2Secondary attribute -1
3–4No change
5Primary attribute +1
6Primary attribute +1 and secondary attribute +1

The GM determines which attributes are primary and secondary for each breed. This roll can change each attribute by no more than 1.

2. Horse Breeds

BreedAttribute BonusesSpecialization

ThoroughbredAgility +2, Condition +1Speed and pursuit

Draft HorseMight +2, Condition +2, Wisdom +1Heavy hauling

Breed bonuses represent natural abilities, not training.

3. Horse Statistics

Hit Points (HP)

HP = 10 + Condition modifier + Breed HP bonus

Horse TypeHP Bonus

At 0 HP, a horse is incapacitated and cannot be ridden or work normally.

Armor DP comes from protective equipment; ordinary saddles and bridles provide none.

  • Thoroughbred: +10 ft. to cantering and galloping.
  • Draft horse: -10 ft. to cantering and galloping.
  • Other breeds: no change.

Extended fast travel may require stamina checks.

Stamina

Maximum Stamina = 6 + Condition modifier

  • Strenuous travel or heavy labor: -1 Stamina per hour.
  • Galloping for a full minute: an additional -1 Stamina.
  • At 0 Stamina: cannot gallop and suffers -2 to physical checks.
  • Rest: recover 2 Stamina per hour with water and reasonable conditions.
  • Full night's rest: restore all Stamina with adequate food, water, and shelter.

The GM may adjust costs for terrain, weather, workload, and condition.

These are provisional game values, not real-world load recommendations. Smaller, injured, or exhausted horses may have lower limits.

Exceeding the comfortable load reduces speed by 10 ft. and costs an additional 1 Stamina per hour. A horse should not carry more than 150% of its comfortable load.

4. Temperament

5. Training

A horse may have multiple training types with GM approval. Training does not eliminate fear, pain, or exhaustion.

6. Riding and Handling

When a task is difficult or dangerous, the GM may call for an Animal Handling check using the normal check rules.

TaskDifficulty

Navigate difficult terrain10

These are suggested difficulties. Failure does not automatically cause a fall; consequences depend on the situation.

  • Mounting: No check for a cooperative horse under normal conditions.
  • Dismounting: No check under normal conditions.
  • Riding armed: Difficult shots or riding at a gallop may require checks or penalties.
  • Falling: The GM may call for an Agility check to land safely; failure uses normal falling-damage rules.

Fear and Panic

Gunfire, predators, fires, injuries, and sudden threats may trigger a Wisdom-based check using the horse's Wisdom modifier.

On success, the horse remains under control. On failure, it may hesitate, flee, rear, or resist commands. Temperament, training, and threat severity affect the outcome. Appropriate combat training may grant a bonus against gunfire-related fear.

The GM determines injury severity, duration, and treatment. HP recovers through rest and appropriate care under the game's healing rules. Serious injuries may require veterinary knowledge or professional treatment.

Horses need regular food, water, rest, grooming, and appropriate hoof care. Neglect can cause sickness and impair recovery. The GM may handle routine care narratively unless survival or ranch management is central to the campaign.

10. Horse Core Rules

  • Horses use the same six attributes and modifier rules as characters.
  • Breed determines natural specialization; individual quality distinguishes horses of the same breed.
  • Temperament affects behavior, while training determines reliable capabilities.
  • HP, DB, speed, stamina, and carrying capacity determine physical performance.
  • Equipment is separate unless included in the purchase price.
  • The GM determines when checks are required and what failure means.
  • Horses can become frightened, exhausted, injured, or sick and require proper care.
  • All horse mechanics must remain compatible with the game's attributes, Action Points, combat, and equipment systems.

Oxen

1. Oxen Creation

Create an ox using these steps:

  1. Choose a breed and apply its attribute bonuses.
  2. Roll 1d6 for individual quality.
  3. Choose or roll its temperament.
  4. Calculate HP, DB, speed, stamina, and pulling capacity.
  5. Record its training, identification, equipment, and price.

Oxen use the same six attributes and modifiers as characters: Might, Agility, Condition, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

Oxen are primarily working animals used for pulling wagons, plowing fields, and hauling heavy supplies. They can be trained to follow commands and work in teams but are not suitable for ordinary riding.

10. Ox Core Rules

  • Oxen use the same six attributes and modifier rules as characters.
  • Breed and individual quality determine natural differences.
  • Temperament affects behavior; training determines reliable working capabilities.
  • HP, DB, speed, stamina, and pulling capacity determine physical performance.
  • Pulling capacity applies to the total load being moved.
  • Teamwork requires suitable training and equipment.
  • Oxen can become frightened, exhausted, injured, or sick and require proper care.
  • All mechanics must remain compatible with the game's attributes, Action Points, combat, and equipment systems.
